newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Australia awaits wage case outcome.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Australia awaits wage case outcome.

text.p: Australian Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said on Thursday he would wait for a decision on a major union wage claim before considering further changes to the Industrial Relations Commission's role.

"I'll just be very interested to see their decision," Reith told Reuters in an interview when asked if the outcome could prompt changes to the role of the commission, Australia's main labour tribunal.
Asked if that meant he would consider further changes, Reith said: "My position is that I'm waiting for the decision."

A spokesman from the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), Australia's top union body, said last week the commission's decision would determine its relevance and role in the new industrial relations environment.

Under Reith, the Liberal-National coalition government has extended the reforms of its Labor predecessor to change the system last year by further emphasising workplace bargaining rather than the "award" wages set centrally by the commission.
"It is an important decision for the commission and for the management of wages policy generally," Reith said.
"The legislation defines a role for the commission, but obviously how the commission implements or carries out its duties will have an impact on the reform."

The ACTU has applied to the commission for an 8.75-percent increase in award rates for all workers not covered by workplace agreements, plus three annual A$20-a-week rises for workers unable to negotiate their own deals.
The government has proposed an alternative A$24-a-week rise spread over three years.

Speaking ahead of the anniversary of the coalition's election win on March 2 last year, Reith said he was pleased with what he had achieved during his first year in the ministry and with the government's performance.

He said the main challenges he faced in the next 12 months were the smooth implementation of the workplace reforms, which parliament passed last November, and the development of a public sector reform plan and general award simplification.

"I think, overall, the government has had a very solid year," Reith said. "There's still lots of things to be done, but by and large we've ticked off on the major items that we nominated before the election."

He responded to criticism that the government's workplace reforms needed to go further by saying there were always people who wanted more, and ruled out the introduction of any further reforms in the coming year.
"We've just done what we said we'd do and now we're getting on with implementation," he said.
"There's been widespread support for what we've done and what you're seeing now is people starting to take up some of the opportunities in the new act.
"So not only have they been saying it's a good step in the right direction, they're also now starting to make use of it."
The implementation of the government's reforms, aimed at further deregulating the labour market and giving unions a less significant role in wage negotiations, began this month.
Reith said the full effect would not be seen for another 12 months to two years.
